column4: رَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ names God as the people’s Lord; with 114:2–3 it restates the section’s Lord-owner-worshipped triad.
مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ gives the people’s Lord the explicit owner-king role; 114:1 and 114:3 supply Rabb and Ilāh beside it.
إِلَٰهِ ٱلنَّاسِ completes 114:1–3: the one who is Lord and King is also the one worshipped.
مَٰلِكَ ٱلْمُلْكِ gives and removes rule and both honors and abases; ownership here actively determines the high and low position developed by the image.
Its question “to whom belongs the dominion today?” answers with the One, the Compeller, making the Day of dīn a day on which ownership is undivided.
On يَوْمَ ٱلدِّينِ no soul “possesses” (تَمْلِكُ) anything for another and the command belongs wholly to God, an exact expansion of 1:4.
It names يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ; 82:19 then specifies its decisive loss of all creaturely possession.
The repeated question intensifies the Day of dīn before 82:19 defines it as God’s day of sole command.
Everyone in heaven and earth comes to the Merciful as an عَبْدًا, directly grounding the prose’s claim that free and enslaved people alike already belong to God.
God has counted and numbered every one; this makes 19:93’s universal servanthood an individually held, not merely collective, relation.
Each will come to Him alone, completing 19:93’s scene of every creature arriving as a servant.
لِيَعْبُدُونِ joins createdness to worship, the precise relation behind being God’s abd by origination.
God neither wants provision from His worshippers nor food; the master does not depend on what His servants supply.
Yusuf joins “only Him worship” with ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ in one command, closely matching iyyāka naʿbudu and dīn.
Yusuf asks whether many separate أَرْبَابٌ are better than God the One, the Compeller, setting competing human-style masters against the sole true owner.
The call refuses taking one another as أَرْبَابًا besides God, directly limiting the human master relation the section traces in Rabb.
Taking rabbis and monks as أَرْبَابًا shows the forbidden transfer of lordly obedience to human religious authorities.
A recipient of revelation may not tell people, “be عِبَادًا لِّى”; even elevated human authority cannot turn people into its own servants.
Pharaoh’s “I am your highest Lord” (رَبُّكُمُ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ) is the tyrant’s false claim to the Rabb-role that belongs to God alone.
The Messiah and near angels do not disdain being عَبْدًا لِّلَّهِ: exalted rank does not cancel creaturely servanthood.
God is ٱلْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ, placing the owner above the abd without the need or lowliness denied in 17:111.
Again He is al-Qahhār above His servants, now in the scene of guardians and death, so ownership reaches the servants’ final return.
God has no helper arising from weakness or lowliness; the source’s owner never occupies the humiliated dependent position of a servant.
The parable explicitly stages عَبْدًا مَّمْلُوكًا unable to do anything against a person given good provision who spends it; it is the section’s owned-slave and providing-owner scene.
The dependent, speechless man is a burden on his مَوْلَاهُ, unlike one who commands justice; the comparison keeps the master-dependent relation concrete while refusing to make it a divine equality.
Those given more provision do not make what their hands possess equal sharers in it; the human ownership scene is used to reject equals being assigned to God.
The parable asks whether people would accept slaves from what their right hands possess as equal partners in their provision; it makes the owner-slave asymmetry argue against partners for God.
God creates cattle “for them” and they become مَٰلِكُونَ of them, directly conjoining creaturely provision, ownership, and herd.
وَذَلَّلْنَٰهَا uses the very tamed/subdued action developed through muzallal: people ride and eat the cattle.
The same tamed herd yields benefits and drink; its final question about gratitude gives the owner’s provision the response the image requires.
Moses calls Pharaoh’s supposed favor the fact that he عَبَّدتَّ the Children of Israel, the Qur’anic human counterpart to the prose’s forced abbadta al-qawma.
Pharaoh’s “did we not raise you among us as a child?” supplies the household-master claim to which Moses answers with enslavement in 26:22.
Pharaoh’s people call Moses and Aaron’s people “servants to us,” displaying the same claimed human domination that the Exodus reverses.
God commands Moses to travel by night with “My servants”; the possessive transfers Israel from Pharaoh’s coerced service to God’s protection.
The rescue from Pharaoh’s house, with its degrading violence against Israel, supplies the oppression behind Moses’s word abbadta in 26:22.
Pharaoh exalts himself, divides the people, and weakens one group; this is dominion exercised as human abasement rather than the just lordship of God.
Pharaoh makes his people light and they obey him, a compact portrait of a ruler manufacturing the submission the image distinguishes from worship of God.
In the master’s house Yusuf calls the one who gave him good lodging رَبِّى, preserving the source’s concrete human sense of Rabb as master of a dwelling.
The pair find her سَيِّدَهَا at the door, materially locating the master-and-household scene invoked in 12:23.
Yusuf says one prisoner will serve wine to his رَبّ, a plain human-master use of the same word the section reads in Rabb.
“Mention me to your rabb” uses rabb for the freed prisoner’s earthly master, distinguishing this household vocabulary from divine lordship.
The king tells the messenger to return to his rabb; this is another concrete human authority carried by Rabb.
Yusuf could not keep his brother under the dīn of the king, showing dīn as the binding rule or jurisdiction of a ruler as well as religious obedience.
Those whom the right hand possesses may seek a contract, and their owner must give them from “the wealth of God”; human possession is placed under God’s prior ownership.
Those whom the right hand possesses ask leave at three private times, making the master’s house and its servants a lived household scene.
The command to worship God includes doing good to those whom the right hand possesses, holding human ownership under worship and ethical care.
Marriage with believing slave women and “some of you are from others” makes legal slave status coexist with shared human and religious standing.
Releasing a neck is named as ascent on the steep way, reversing the enslaving and lowering side of the image.
The bee is told to travel the paths of its Lord as ذُلُلًا, bringing the section’s made-easy/tamed road together with a working creature.
The required cow is لَّا ذَلُولٌ for ploughing or watering the field, a deliberate negative boundary for the tamed animal sense of muzallal.
God makes the earth ذَلُولًا: people walk its paths and eat His provision, extending the tamed road image to the inhabited ground itself.
On the backs of ships and animals people remember the One who subjected them for us, making riding an acknowledgment that human control was given.
The Creator made ships and cattle for people to ride; 43:13 turns that created utility into praise of the One who subjected it.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding and adornment, supplying the image’s owned horse with its Qur’anic creaturely source.
Paradise’s fruit clusters are made low and accessible, applying tadhlīl to provision rather than to an animal or person.
Cattle give drink, food, many benefits, and transport, a full animal-provision scene whose usefulness rests on God’s making it available.
God made cattle so that people ride some and eat some, repeating the bodily uses of the subdued herd.
Their further benefits carry people to destinations; this extends 40:79’s ride-and-food scene to transport and travel.
God subjects what is on earth and the ship moving by His command, identifying all workable ground and transport as held under divine command.
God subjects what is in the heavens and earth and lavishes visible and hidden favors, broadening the tamed creature to a fitted world.
Everything in the heavens and earth is subjected from Him, the comprehensive form of the animal and ground made usable for people.
All in heaven and earth submit to God willingly or unwillingly under His دِين, making the created servant’s belonging antecedent to a chosen verbal confession.
At the covenant God asks, “Am I not your رَبّ?” and they answer yes; it stages the creature’s own acknowledgment of the Lord relation later voiced in worship.
“Innā lillāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn” puts belonging to God and return to Him in the servants’ own voice.
God addresses “My believing servants” (عِبَادِي) and says “Me alone worship”; possession by Him and the direct answer of worship stand in one sentence.
God’s covenant forbids worshipping Satan, an enemy master, setting a rival obedience relation against the service owed to God.
“Worship Me” follows 36:60 and calls it a straight way, giving the positive master-servant response after the rejected service of Satan.
God speaks in the first person—there is no god but Me, so فَٱعْبُدْنِى—an especially close counterpart to the turn from “He” to “You” in 1:5.
Every messenger is sent with “there is no god but Me, so فَٱعْبُدُونِ,” combining the sole worshipped one with direct divine address.
“Worship God, making the دِين sincere for Him” joins the two named roots as exclusive allegiance.
“The pure دِين belongs to God” presents dīn as an allegiance whose rightful owner is God.
The Prophet is commanded to worship God while making the dīn sincere for Him, keeping worship and dīn together in a speaking servant’s obedience.
“God I worship, making my dīn sincere for Him” gives the worshipper’s explicit first-person acceptance of that allegiance.
People are commanded only to worship God, sincere to Him in the دِين; the verse recasts the image’s obedience as an exclusive religious act.
“I do not worship what you worship” marks a concrete refusal to give the act of service to another claimed object of worship.
“You are not worshippers of what I worship” identifies the opposing service relation in the exchange.
“Your dīn for you and my dīn for me” names the separated allegiances after the reciprocal refusals of worship.
Those worshipped besides God cannot control provision; the verse redirects the seeker to God for provision, worship, and thanks, undoing false ownership.
Sun and moon are not to be prostrated to; worship belongs to their Creator, who owns the objects people might otherwise elevate.
God is Creator of everything and is therefore to be worshipped (فَٱعْبُدُوهُ); creation is stated as the warrant for service.
The believer asks why he should not worship the One who originated him and to whom he returns, making creation and return the grounds of worship.
“Your Rabb has decreed that you worship none but Him” directly binds the Lord-title to exclusive obedience.
Every community receives the command to worship God and avoid tāghūt, framing worship as a choice between the true master and coercive rivals.
Jesus says God is “my Rabb and your Rabb, so worship Him,” joining shared Lordship and worship in the same address.
The angels are عِبَادٌ مُّكْرَمُونَ: their honor lies with, rather than above, service, answering the prose’s secondary honored sense.
All in the heavens and earth belong to Him, and those near Him do not scorn His worship; proximity intensifies rather than cancels servanthood.
Those with your Lord do not grow too proud for His worship, but glorify and prostrate; the abd’s lowliness is enacted without degrading God.
God takes His عَبْدِهِ by night on an honored journey, a narrative in which the named servant is distinguished and cared for.
The Criterion is sent down to God’s عَبْدِهِ, combining the servant name with a high prophetic commission.
A servant from among God’s servants receives mercy and divinely taught knowledge, showing service alongside special honor and gift.
Jesus says “I am the servant of God” while recounting the Book and prophethood given to him; divinely favored status remains abd-status.
Jesus is only a servant upon whom God bestowed favor, a direct correction of elevating a favored servant into a lord.
God is sufficient for His servant; the master’s sufficiency answers the dependent servant’s need for help in 1:5.
God is gentle with His servants and provides for whom He wills, rendering the owner’s care and provision without reducing Him to a human master.
People are needy toward God while He is the Self-Sufficient, Praised; this makes divine lordship unlike possession that depends on its servants.
The satisfied soul is invited to enter “among My servants” (عِبَادِي), portraying final acceptance and honor inside belonging to God.
God honors the children of Adam and carries/provides for them, keeping human dignity within the universal creaturely dependence described by the image.
Satan has no authority over God’s servants except followers who go astray, drawing a boundary around which master may command them.
God repeats that Satan has no authority over “My servants,” then names the Lord sufficient as guardian, adding protection to divine possession.
God’s servants drink from a spring they make flow abundantly, a provision scene in which the servant is received and supplied.
The righteous servants inherit the earth: divine ownership can honor servants with inheritance rather than leave them in a permanently low human status.
The question asks who holds the مَلَكُوت of everything in His hand, protects, and cannot be protected against; ownership is absolute command and shelter.
Everything’s مَلَكُوت is in God’s hand and all return to Him, extending hand-held ownership to the creature’s final destination.
Blessed is the One in whose hand is ٱلْمُلْك and who is powerful over every thing, a direct account of Mālik as effective possession.
The dominion of heavens and earth belongs to God, who creates and apportions children, linking ownership to origination and gift.
The keys of the heavens and earth belong to God, rendering His ownership through the concrete possession of access and stores.
His is the dominion; He gives life and death, so the master’s possession governs the servants’ existence rather than merely their goods.
The dying are challenged: if you are not مَدِينِينَ, subject to authority or requital, why cannot you reverse death in 56:87?
“Bring it back, if you are truthful” supplies the powerless human test that exposes the claim of being outside dīn in 56:86.
The question whether the dead will be madīnūn invokes being brought under reckoning, carrying dīn from present obedience into its final consequence.
Face the upright dīn according to God’s originating fitrah; it links true allegiance to the way God constituted humanity.
Alleged partners legislate a dīn God did not permit, showing rival authorities attempting to claim the master’s right to prescribe obedience.
Denying the dīn opens the passage whose person repels the orphan and withholds food, setting refusal of final accountability against responsibility for those without power.
